summary: Describes a detailed model of IPv4 multicast with RSVP, built using the OPNET simulation package, with protocol procedures written in C. Researchers can use it to study how these protocols behave. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a pretend version of a network, built on a computer, for testing how sending to many receivers works with reserved bandwidth.

how does the simulation model multicast and rsvp
subtitle: A computer model for testing multicast and quality-of-service protocols.

tldr.problem: Researchers need a way to study how IP multicast and RSVP (resource reservation) protocols behave before deploying them in real networks.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC describes a detailed simulation model built using the OPNET tool that recreates IPv4 multicast, RSVP, and various routing protocols (OSPF, MOSPF, DVMRP) in software.
tldr.outcome: The model is made publicly available to the multicast research community for testing protocol behavior, analyzing performance constraints, and validating designs before real-world deployment.

today: RFC 2490 is an Informational RFC that documents a simulation model made available to the research community. It remains a reference for those studying multicast and RSVP protocol behavior through simulation.

sections.title: Background and Purpose
sections.content:
The RFC describes a simulation model for IPv4 multicast with RSVP, built using the OPNET (Optimized Network Engineering Tools) simulation package. The model was created to fill a gap: while RSVP developers had used simulation during design, no general-purpose simulation of IP multicast with RSVP was widely available for the research community.

IP multicast allows a single packet to reach multiple receivers efficiently, and RSVP allows applications to reserve network resources to guarantee quality of service. The combination is important for real-time applications like video, voice, and distributed simulation.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you want to send one message to lots of people at the same time, and you want to promise it will arrive quickly. This describes how to pretend to do that in a computer, so scientists can test if their ideas work.

sections.title: The OPNET Simulation Environment
sections.content:
The model is built using OPNET, a commercial discrete-event simulation tool that models networks as interconnected components. Each component's behavior is described as a state-transition diagram with C language code. OPNET layers are modular with well-defined interfaces, making the models portable to other simulation environments.

The architecture includes network layer (routers, links, subnets), node layer (hosts and routers with protocol stacks), and process layer (individual protocol behavior). The model is compatible with OPNET 3.5.
sections.plainLanguage: The simulation breaks a network into pieces, each showing what it does in different situations. Each piece has a rule written in a programming language.

sections.title: IP Multicast and IGMP Implementation
sections.content:
The model implements IP multicast with IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol) for hosts to join and leave multicast groups. Routers maintain unicast and multicast routing tables, plus group membership tables updated by IGMP.

IGMP queries are sent periodically to determine group membership. When a host joins a group, it sends a response; when the last host leaves, the router removes the group from that interface. The model includes both FDDI ring and Ethernet subnets with proper handling of multicast at the link layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts raise their hands when they want to hear about a group. Routers ask periodically if anyone is still listening. When the last hand goes down, the router stops sending to that place.

sections.title: RSVP and Routing Protocols
sections.content:
The model implements RSVP using fixed-filter reservation style, with support for path messages, reservation messages, path teardown, and reservation teardown. Routers maintain path state blocks (PSBs) and reservation state blocks (RSBs) to track sender information and receiver requirements.

Three multicast routing protocols are included: OSPF/MOSPF (for interior routing with multicast support), DVMRP (Distance Vector Multicast Routing Protocol), and basic unicast routing (RIP or OSPF). Routers use reverse path forwarding to build spanning trees for each multicast group.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP works like making a reservation: a sender says what it will send, receivers say what they need, and routers promise to deliver it. Different routing protocols find different paths through the network.

sections.title: Performance and Scalability
sections.content:
The RFC documents simulation performance on a SGI Octane workstation with 512 MB memory. Three test configurations are described:

Debug Model: 11 routers, 12 hosts, simulating 100 seconds takes 3 hours real time; 200 seconds takes 7 hours.

Intermediate Model: 42 routers, 48 hosts, simulating 100 seconds takes 14 hours; 200 seconds takes 30 hours.

Large Model: 86 routers, 96 hosts, simulating 100 seconds takes 30 hours.

The model has demonstrated good scalability and is made publicly available to support expanded studies of resource-reserved multicasting.
sections.plainLanguage: Pretending a whole network exists takes a long time on a real computer. A small pretend network of 11 routers takes 3 hours of computer time to simulate 100 seconds of real network time.
